title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
description:
# Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed

Implement the `RandomizedCollection` class. It behaves like a multiset, so the same value may be stored more than once.

*   `RandomizedCollection()` initializes an empty collection.
*   `boolean insert(int val)` inserts one occurrence of `val`. Return `true` if the collection did not contain `val` before this insertion, otherwise return `false`.
*   `boolean remove(int val)` removes exactly one occurrence of `val` if any occurrence exists. Return `true` if an occurrence was removed, otherwise return `false`.
*   `int getRandom()` returns a uniformly random occurrence from the current collection. Therefore a value with `k` occurrences is `k` times as likely to be returned as a value with one occurrence. The collection is guaranteed to be nonempty when this method is called.

Every operation must run in average `O(1)` time.

Example random returns show one possible outcome. In `[1,1,2]`, return `1` with probability `2/3` and `2` with probability `1/3`.

In operation examples, the first array lists operations and the second lists their argument lists, paired by index and executed left to right. The first operation constructs the object; later operations use that same object. Outputs align by index too: constructors and void methods produce `null`; an empty argument list `[]` means no arguments.

## Example 1:

**Input**
["RandomizedCollection", "insert", "insert", "insert", "getRandom", "remove", "getRandom"]
[[], [1], [1], [2], [], [1], []]
**Output**
[null, true, false, true, 2, true, 1]

**Explanation:** After inserting `1`, `1`, and `2`, the first `getRandom` returns `1` with probability `2/3` and `2` with probability `1/3`. Removing `1` deletes only one occurrence, so the remaining collection contains one `1` and one `2`.

## Constraints:

*   `-2^31 <= val <= 2^31 - 1`
*   At most `2 * 10^5` calls will be made to `insert`, `remove`, and `getRandom`.
*   There will be at least one element in the data structure when `getRandom` is called.

solutions.name: ArrayList With LinkedHashSet Index Buckets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store every occurrence in an `ArrayList<Integer>`. For each value, keep a `LinkedHashSet<Integer>` of dense indexes that currently contain that value. Removing one occurrence picks an index from that set, moves the final occurrence into that index, updates the moved value's index set, and removes the list tail.

## Key Insight

Duplicates mean the map cannot store one index per value. It must store all occurrence indexes, while the dense list makes `getRandom` proportional to occurrence count because each occurrence owns one random slot.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Dynamic Int Array With Index Sets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use a manually growing `int[]` for dense occurrence storage and a hash map from value to a set of indexes. Insert writes the next dense slot. Remove updates the value's index set, swaps the final dense value into the removed slot when needed, and updates the moved value's set.

## Key Insight

The multiset version uses the same dense-index invariant as RandomizedSet, but each value maps to many indexes. The array implementation makes the occurrence slots explicit.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation; array growth is amortized.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Dense Slot HashMaps With Index Sets
solutions.description:
## Approach

Emulate the dense array with `indexToValue`, and store every value's dense indexes in `valueToIndices`. Removal chooses one stored index, moves the last dense slot into that index, fixes the moved value's index set, deletes the old tail slot, and removes empty value buckets.

## Key Insight

A physical array is not required; what matters is the logical dense slot range. Two hash-map layers make the dense slots and per-value occurrence index sets visible as separate concepts.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Occurrence Entry Dense Array
solutions.description:
## Approach

Represent each occurrence as an `Entry` object containing its value and current dense index. A map from value to a set of entries lets `remove` choose one occurrence. Removing swaps the last entry into the removed entry's index and updates the moved entry's stored index.

## Key Insight

For duplicates, each occurrence can be treated as its own record. That keeps duplicate values separate without needing to store raw integer indexes in the value bucket.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).

solutions.name: Index Bag With Back Pointers
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store dense values in an `ArrayList`, but replace each value's `HashSet<Integer>` with a custom `IndexBag`. The bag stores its indexes in a dense list and a map from index to position inside that list, so adding, removing any known index, and picking an arbitrary index are all O(1) average.

## Key Insight

The per-value index set is itself a small design problem. A back-pointer bag makes the set operations explicit and avoids relying on `HashSet` iteration details for the teaching route.

## Complexity Analysis
- Time Complexity: O(1) average per operation.
- Space Complexity: O(n).
